title: Cortical Excitatory Neurons
intro: About four out of five neurons in the neocortex are excitatory, and almost all of them are pyramidal cells or their close relatives. They are the only cortical cells whose axons leave the local circuit, so everything a column computes reaches the rest of the brain through them. Their layer, their shape and above all where their axon projects divide them into a handful of classes with different jobs.

items: Glutamate as transmitter, acting on AMPA and NMDA receptors of their targets.
Spiny dendrites: each spine usually carries one excitatory synapse, and a pyramidal cell has thousands to tens of thousands of them.
Regular spiking with adaptation as the default firing pattern, with bursting in some layer 5 and some layer 2/3 cells.
Low, skewed firing rates in vivo: most fire below a few Hz, a few fire much more (Buzsaki & Mizuseki 2014).

Sparse, weak and highly specific connections to one another: a pair of nearby pyramidal cells is connected with probability of roughly 0.05 to 0.2, and a single synapse moves the target by under a millivolt.

Class   Where the soma is   Where the axon goes                  Page
------  ------------------  -----------------------------------  ----------------------
IT      L2/3, L4, L5, L6    other cortex (both hemispheres),     L2/3 Pyramidal,
                            striatum; never leaves telencephalon  L4 Spiny Stellate
PT/ET   L5 (L5b)            brainstem, spinal cord, thalamus,    L5 Pyramidal
                            superior colliculus, striatum
CT      L6                  thalamus (and back to L4 / L6)       L6 Corticothalamic
NP      L5/L6               mostly local, little long-range      (see L6 page)

IT = intratelencephalic, PT = pyramidal tract, ET = extratelencephalic,
CT = corticothalamic, NP = near-projecting (Harris & Shepherd 2015).

blocks.text: Harris and Shepherd (2015) argue that these projection classes are the deeper division, more fundamental than layer. IT cells exist in every layer and form the cortex-to-cortex network; PT cells are found only in layer 5 and carry the cortex's commands to subcortical motor and sensory structures; CT cells sit in layer 6 and regulate the thalamus. Transcriptomic atlases (Tasic et al. 2018) recover the same split.

items: Layer 2/3 Pyramidal Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-excitatory/l23-pyramidal): the main cortico-cortical cells, sparse firing, many recurrent connections.
Layer 4 Spiny Stellate Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-excitatory/l4-spiny-stellate): the input layer's local excitatory cells, driven by the thalamus.
Layer 5 Pyramidal Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-excitatory/l5-pyramidal): thick-tufted bursting output cells and slender-tufted IT cells, with the most studied dendrites in the brain.
Layer 6 Corticothalamic Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-excitatory/l6-corticothalamic): the feedback cells that tune the thalamus and layer 4.

blocks.text: Large network models usually give every excitatory class the same point-neuron model and let layer-specific connectivity do the work (Potjans & Diesmann 2014 use one LIF for all eight populations). Models that care about cell types swap in class-specific parameters: the Allen Institute's V1 model (Billeh et al. 2020) uses GLIF parameters fitted to recorded cells of each excitatory class, and Blue Brain's microcircuit uses separate detailed models for 13 excitatory m-types. A sensible middle ground for a spiking column is Izhikevich or AdEx regular-spiking cells in layers 2/3, 4 and 6, and bursting cells with a dendritic compartment in layer 5.
